The Devonian Period. Running from four hundred and nineteen to three hundred and fifty-nine million years ago, the Devonian is called the Age of Fishes because jawed fish diversified explosively and dominated the oceans. Meanwhile, plants carpeted the land with forests, and the first four-legged vertebrates—tetrapods—crawled from the water onto dry land. The period takes its name from Devon, a county in southwest England.

The Age of Fishes saw the rise of sharks, ray-finned fish, and lobe-finned fish—the latter being the ancestors of all land vertebrates. Tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fish, and fossils like Tiktaalik and Acanthostega show the transition between aquatic and terrestrial life. Vast forests of early trees—ferns, club mosses, and seed-ferns—covered the continents, producing the first significant oxygen surge from land plants.

The Devonian extinction came in pulses, striking around three hundred and seventy-five million years ago and again at the period's end three hundred and fifty-nine million years ago, wiping out reef-building corals and many fish species, possibly from ocean anoxia or an asteroid impact. Lobe-finned fish had fleshy fins and lungs, giving them the anatomical toolkit to eventually colonise land. The first insects appeared during this period, diversifying on the newly vegetated landscape.

The Devonian connects to the Silurian Period before it, when vascular plants first emerged, and to the Carboniferous Period that followed, when tetrapods radiated into great diversity.
